newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Ross disputes claims on Solomons gold mine.
newsitem.headline: Ross disputes claims on Solomons gold mine.

text.p: Ross Mining NL said it was confident its proposed A$61.1 million gold mine in the Solomon Islands would proceed despite new landowner compensation claims.

Ross' chief executive Bertus de Graaf was responding in a statement to claims on Wednesday by a landowner leader that the project had the potential to become a disaster similar to the closed Bougainville mine in Papua New Guinea (PNG).
The paramount chief of the leading tribe opposing the venture, Willie Ronie, said in a letter to Ross shareholders that at least 20 other landowners had now started legal action against Ross.

The compensation package which Ross was offering landowners --- a 1.5 percent royalty on gold production, A$2.3 million for relocation of the village, A$1.46 million for loss of land and income and 0.0015 percent of the company in shares --- was "ridiculously low", Ronie said.
Lihir Gold Ltd's compensation package for its new mine at the eastern end of PNG was much more generous, he said.

It involved a 1.5 percent gross royalty, a 7.5 percent free carried interest in Lihir Gold for all Lihirans, establishment of a business development group controlled by landowners, supply of all food, catering, transport and vehicles by Lihirans, purchase of A$4 million worth of heavy earthmoving equipment for two Lihir tribes which act as earthmoving contractors, a A$40 million housing trust fund and a policy of employment preference for Lihirans, he said.
"The deal Ross Mining has put to us is obviously at the bottom end of the scale and we will not accept it," he said.

The same chain of events was unfolding for the proposed Ross mine as occurred 300 miles west on Bougainville Island, where the world's largest copper mine was closed because landowners' claims on compensation, pollution and destruction were ignored, he said.

Ross Mining's de Graaf said the claim, which was being brought by only one landowner from the mine area together with a Guadalcanal resident well away from mining operations, was based on misinformation and made no allegations on environmental issues.
It also made no claim for damages or compensation.
"We will ... deal with the issues in court," he said.
Ronie was until six weeks ago a vocal supporter of the project and an enthusiastic signatory to the compensation agreement, de Graaf said.
"We do not respond to threats," he said.
Tailings and waste would not be released into the local river but would be contained at the mine site in accordance with Australian best practice, he said.
